extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy, constitutional theorists, and legislators interested in principles of legitimate government
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and principles governing legitimate legislative, executive, and federative authority in a commonwealth, including limits on lawmaking, property/taxation rules, separation of powers, representation, and executive prerogative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consent as foundation of law
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws require the consent of the society; no body can make laws for a people without their consent and authority received from them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All obedience ultimately terminates in the supreme power derived from societal consent. Citations: 'the consent of the society... is absolutely necessary to its being a law.' (Hooker referenced.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative power limited to powers transferred
rubrics_metrics.description: The legislative can have no more power than individuals had in the state of nature and consented to give; it cannot be absolutely arbitrary over lives and fortunes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because nobody can transfer more power than they possess, the legislature's power is limited to what men gave up for preservation; it 'is limited to the public good of the society' and cannot rightfully destroy, enslave, or impoverish subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws must conform to the law of nature (and God)
rubrics_metrics.description: Human laws must be measured by higher rules — the law of God and the law of nature — and cannot be good or valid against the fundamental law of preservation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The obligations of the law of nature do not cease in society; municipal laws must not contradict the law of nature or positive scripture. (References to Hooker.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Govern by promulgated standing laws and known judges
rubrics_metrics.description: The legislative cannot rule by extemporary arbitrary decrees but is bound to dispense justice through promulgated standing laws and known authorized judges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without established laws and judges, disputes and rights cannot be reliably determined; reliance on unwritten natural law alone allows misapplication and disorder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality before the law (one rule for rich and poor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws should be established and promulgated so as to be the same rule for rich and poor, favourites at court and countrymen at plough.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Established, uniform rules secure duty-knowledge for people and keep rulers within bounds; laws must not be varied in particular cases to favour some.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative ends limited to public good and preservation
rubrics_metrics.description: The ultimate end of legislation is the good of the people — preservation of life, liberty, and property — and the legislative has no other end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any power exercised beyond preservation (e.g., to destroy or impoverish) is illegitimate; the trust of legislators is fiduciary toward public welfare.

rubrics_metrics.name: No taking of private property without consent
rubrics_metrics.description: The supreme power cannot take from any man any part of his property without his own consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Property is the reason for entering society; taking property without consent would negate property itself. Taxes and takings require the consent of the majority or their representatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxation requires consent of the people
rubrics_metrics.description: It is fit everyone who enjoys protection should pay proportionally, but taxation must be with his own consent — the consent of the majority given by themselves or their deputies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A ruler who levies taxes by his own authority invades the fundamental law of property and subverts government ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative cannot transfer lawmaking power
rubrics_metrics.description: The legislative cannot transfer the power of making laws to any other hands; the people alone can appoint who shall make laws for them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative authority is a delegated, positive grant from the people and does not include the power to make new legislators or delegate lawmaking elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of legislative and executive to prevent abuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the same persons making laws and executing them is a temptation to abuse, well-ordered commonwealths separate legislative and executive powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separation ensures lawmakers are again subject to the laws they make; executive must often be always in being whereas legislature need not be.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive must be always in being
rubrics_metrics.description: While the legislative need not be always in being, it is necessary that the executive power be always in being to see to the execution of laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Execution of laws is a continuous need; thus an enduring executive ensures laws are carried into effect when legislature is not sitting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federative power for war/peace and foreign affairs
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a federative power concerning war and peace, leagues and alliances — management of relations with foreign persons and communities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This federative power is less capable of direction by standing laws and must largely be left to the prudence and wisdom of those entrusted with it for the public good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of public force — practical limits on separating executive/federative
rubrics_metrics.description: Though executive and federative are distinct in nature, they are hardly practicably separable because both require the force of the commonwealth and unity of command.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Placing the force under distinct, non-subordinate hands risks disorder and ruin; practical governance often unites these powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: People retain supreme power to remove abusive legislative
rubrics_metrics.description: Even in a constituted commonwealth the people keep a supreme power to remove or alter the legislative when it acts contrary to trust and the ends of preservation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All delegated power limited by its trust reverts to the people when the end is manifestly neglected; this justifies resistance or removal of legislators who invade liberties and properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of force without authority is a state of war
rubrics_metrics.description: If the executive uses force to hinder the meeting or acting of the legislative without authority, that is a state of war with the people who may oppose by force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proper remedy to force without authority is to oppose force to it; aggressors employing force without authority become liable to be treated as in a state of war.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive's power to convoke/dissolve legislature is fiduciary
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of assembling and dismissing the legislative placed in the executive is a fiduciary trust, not a superiority over the legislature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prerogative exists because framers cannot foresee all future exigencies; it should be exercised only for the public weal, not by arbitrary good pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation must be proportionate and adaptable
rubrics_metrics.description: Representation that in time becomes unequal and disproportionate to the reasons it was established upon is an injustice that may be rectified to restore true representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where custom has ossified representation (e.g., decayed towns still overrepresented), correcting representation to reflect assistance to the public is justified and 'an undoubted friend to, and establisher of the government.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Subordinate powers are delegated and accountable
rubrics_metrics.description: Ministerial and subordinate powers have no authority beyond what is delegated by positive grant and are accountable to some other power in the commonwealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such officers' powers are limited by commission and subject to oversight; the legislature can resume execution or punish maladministration when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive prerogative to act for public good beyond law
rubrics_metrics.description: The executive has prerogative — power to act according to discretion for the public good in cases where municipal law gives no direction, and sometimes even against the law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the legislature cannot foresee all accidents, the executive may mitigate severity of laws, pardon offenders, or take measures (e.g., stop a spreading fire) when strict law would do harm; prerogative must be used to preserve the members of society.
